extracted.intended_audience: British policymakers, missionaries, colonial administrators, and general readers concerned with West African administration (late 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A late-19th-century essay-style critique of missionary practice, labour policy, and education in West Africa arguing how administration, missionary methods, and training should be changed to develop native labour and society. It mixes empirical observations, chemical/medical notes, and ethnological claims to support policy prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imported labour suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Even had the experiment of imported labour been successful for the time being, I hold it would be a grave error to import labour into Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mortality and treatment evidence (e.g., Annamese gang mortality) to judge imported-labour experiments; favour developing native labour because "Africa possesses in herself the most magnificent mass of labour material"; imported labour experiments that produce very high mortality (e.g., 70% in one Annamese gang) count as failures and counsel against further importation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for good guidance and proper management
rubrics_metrics.description: But good guidance and proper management are the things that are wanted--and are wanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy success depends on appropriate governance and training regimes rather than simple importation of labour; point to Krumen example as evidence that training and management can unlock native labour potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate missionary pedagogy (avoid 'emptying and refilling')
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure of the missionary to recognise the difference between the African and themselves as being a difference not of degree but of kind...regarding the native minds as so many jugs only requiring to be emptied of the stuff which is in them and refilled with the particular form of dogma he is engaged in teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missionary instruction should not treat natives as blank slates; avoid methods that simply replace native customs with imported dogma. Anti-pattern: 'emptying and refilling' pedagogy that removes local restraints without providing suitable replacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of conversion/education (avoid superficial conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not converted in the least. ... those Africans who are the chief mainstay of missionary reports ... have merely had the restraint of fear removed from their minds without the greater restraint of love being put in its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate missionary success by the moral and social depth of change (love/ethical transformation), not just attendance, baptisms, or elementary literacy. Superficial indicators (baptisms, church attendance) do not equal true conversion or social improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social integration outcomes of education
rubrics_metrics.description: The missionary-made man is the curse of the Coast... The pagans despise him, the whites hate him, still he thinks enough of himself to keep him comfortable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing a class alienated from both their own people and Europeans; measure education by whether it yields socially integrated, respected individuals rather than conceited, marginal figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating polygamy in African societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Polygamy for the African is not an unmixed evil; and that at the present culture-level of the African it is not to be eradicated. ... it is perfectly impossible for one African woman to do the work of the house, prepare the food, fetch water, cultivate the plantations, and look after the children attributive to one man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess customary practices like polygamy in their socioeconomic context (labour needs, division of labour) rather than by imported moral prejudice; policy aiming at eradication should consider practical domestic labour demands and ethnological facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing liquor traffic by evidence not sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The missionary party on the whole have gravely exaggerated both the evil and the extent of the liquor traffic in West Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base judgments about alcohol harms and prevalence on calm investigation and government/statistical reports rather than emotional missionary anecdotes or publicity-seeking claims. Anti-pattern: repeating dramatic but unverified tales to solicit subscriptions or outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical analysis of imported spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: An analysis of trade-gin shows it 'differs in no material particulars from, and was neither more nor less deleterious to health than, gin purchased in different parts of London.' (composition listed: absolute alcohol 39.35%, traces of ethers, aldehydes, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chemical/forensic evidence to evaluate claims that trade spirits are 'poisonous' or uniquely deleterious; accusations of 'raw alcohol' should be tested by laboratory analysis rather than rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual understanding of alcohol use
rubrics_metrics.description: The liquor goes in at a few ports... is diffused ... used as a buying medium, for fetish-worship, and because of climate and food conditions natives desire stimulants; palm wine and other native intoxicants have particular health effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess alcohol consumption in relation to trade practices, religious/ritual uses, climate-induced needs for stimulants, and available alternatives; interventions should account for these contexts (e.g., spirits sometimes replace worse local intoxicants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Align vocational training with local labor demand
rubrics_metrics.description: What Africa wants at present, and will want for the next 200 years at least, are workers, planters, plantation hands, miners, and seamen; and there are no schools in Africa to teach these things or the doctrine of the nobility of labour save the technical mission-schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design technical and vocational education to meet concrete, local economic needs (manual trades and industries) rather than producing clerks or teaching crafts not in demand. Anti-pattern: mission/technical schools emphasizing bookbinding, printing, tailoring where not needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a surplus clerical class
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as an African learns to read and write he turns into a clerk. Now there is no immediate use for clerks in Africa, certainly no room for further development in this line of goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational policy should not push large numbers into clerical roles that the local economy cannot absorb; emphasize 'nobility of labour' and practical skills instead of producing unemployed or underemployed clerks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use industrial missions to develop faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: An industrial mission would be so valuable to the spiritual cause, for by employing and amusing the largely preponderating lower faculties of the African's mind, it would give the higher faculties time to develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine industrial (work-based) training with spiritual instruction: occupying and training lower faculties aids overall character and skill development. Example: missions that include technical employment can sustain early enthusiasm and lead to durable gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question craniology and physiological determinism for policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole attempt to make out that the African is a child-form, 'an arrested development,' is--well, not supported by facts. ... for practical purposes such considerations as weight of brain, or closure of sutures, etc., are negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base administrative or educational policy on crude craniological metrics or strict physiological determinism; rely instead on observable teachability, practical performance, and contextual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical aptitude and teachability (trainable with correct methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The African is almost as teachable and as willing to learn handicrafts as he is to assimilate other things, provided his mind has not been poisoned by fallacious ideas, and the results already obtained from the Krumen and the Accras are good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate native capacity by practical apprenticeship and technical training outcomes (Krumen, Accras examples); do not assume incapacity — selection of appropriate training methods can yield good results. Anti-pattern: assuming mechanical inability and therefore not investing in vocational training.
